obtained.how: the Internet Archive item biostor-194387 (BioStor's scan of the article from the Biodiversity Heritage Library's Zoologica volume, with a text layer), openly downloadable; BHL's own part-PDF link refused the script

bibliography.checked_against: the article's first page and running heads (Zoologica XXIV:25, pp. 367–378, plates I–II) and the BHL part record (doi:10.5962/p.203644)
bibliography.note: the author is 'C. M. Breder, Jr.' (New York Aquarium); '25' is the article's number within volume 24, not an issue number. Adding doi:10.5962/p.203644 (BHL) would give the entry a link

claims.claim: incubation 6–10 d (mean 8) at 21.3 °C; the code's '8 d at 21.3 °C'
claims.location: p. 374 (PDF p. 8), Table II (read on the page image)
claims.conditions: Table II pools seven nests: four aquarium nests of 1931–1934 (data from Breder 1935, 6–10 d at 21.1–23.3 °C) and the three 1939 outdoor-pool nests (Mahwah, N.J.; 7, 7 and 9 (corrected 7) d at 20.8 °C). 21.3 °C is the mean of the nests' mean temperatures, not one rearing temperature; the mean is printed '8—', just under 8
claims.note: the digits are the table's summary row. Better wording: '6–10 d (mean 8) at nest means of 20.8–23.3 °C (mean 21.3)'

claims.claim: nests in an excavation or burrow at 0.2–1.2 m (with Armstrong 1962)
claims.location: p. 374 (PDF p. 8), Table II; p. 368 (PDF p. 2)
claims.conditions: 7–48 in. = 0.18–1.22 m. The 48-in. depth is that of the four aquarium nests (Breder 1935); the 1939 pool nests lay at 28, 16 and 7 in. (0.7, 0.4 and 0.2 m)
claims.note: the 1.2-m upper end is an aquarium depth, so the field range in this source is 0.2–0.7 m; the 1939 nests were a flower pot and two open saucer-shaped excavations 'not unlike those of centrarchids', the species usually nesting in cavities

claims.claim: spawning after a slow rise to ~21 °C; ~3-mm eggs
claims.note: not in Breder 1939, which gives no spawning trigger or egg size (its fish were stocked 26 April and laid eggs 22/24, 27 and 29 June, Table I). By egg_stage.md both come from Breder 1935; cite that alone for them

claims.quote: only one parent incubated where a nest was built in the open
claims.conditions: three first-time spawning pairs in a 1939 outdoor pool; in each nest one parent, thought to be the female, did all the incubating; both parents attended nest 1's young after hatching; in Breder's earlier aquarium fish both parents incubated, and in the field broods are seen with two attendants or one
claims.source_value: single-parent incubation in all three 1939 nests; biparental incubation only in the earlier aquarium pairs (Breder 1935) and some field broods
claims.note: 'biparental' may stand as a general description (Breder 1935; Blumer via ADW: both parents in 56 % of broods), but not on Breder 1939's authority

Breder 1939 says only that eggs 'could not be hatched artificially without considerable agitation', citing Eycleshymer (1901) and Breder (1935) (p. 375, PDF p. 9), and finds that tail-fanning alone was enough in nest 1 (Summary 2, p. 376). The < 24 h is Breder 1935 ('All eggs died in less than twenty-four hours in standing water', that paper's p. 8 of the PDF): cite 1935

tried.note: BHL refused the script (the Internet Archive copy was used)

notes: Other values in the paper: days to swim-up 1–16 (mean 7+, corrected 8) and 10–26 d in the nest (mean 15) — Table II; nests spaced as far apart as the pool allowed, out of sight of each other; broods of neighbouring nests mixed from swim-up; Table I (p. 373, read on the page image): eggs 24 (probably 22), 27 and 29 June, hatched 3 (probably 29 June), 4 and 6 July, young off the nests 4–11 July, family schools broke up from 14 July, pair 1 still gave slight attention on 20 August and care had fully ceased by 26 August. The paper's Table 3.6-1 credits the incubation timing to 'Breder 1935, 1939' — fine, since Table II pools both, but the pool nests alone ran 7–9 d at 20.8 °C.
